Nevertheless, the above alludes to some of those whom the Prophet addressed by saying, My Lord knows best their number. For He said, ma yaʿlamuhu as opposed to la yaʿlamuhu. This indicates negation of the circumstantial phrase followed by an exception to it by saying, except for a few (illā qalīl), thus rendering a positive

circumstantial meaning. What springs to mind is that they were some of the People of the Book.

In sum, this means that the three opinions were in circulation during the time of the Prophet. Thus, sa-yaqulūna thalāthatun (some will say three) is indicative of the future. Similarly, so are, wa yaquluna khamsatun (some say five), and, wa yaquluna sabʿatun (some say seven) since they are joined with “and” (wa) to the phrase containing a verb with the prefix for the future tense, which mean the near future in relation to the time when the verses were revealed or the time when the incident occurred, so take note of this.

Therefore, contend not (fa lā tumāri) in their matter but with an outward contention (illa mirāʾan ẓāhiran): Al-Rāghib says that:

“Miryah means hesitation about something, and that it has a narrower meaning than shakk (doubt, uncertainty). Imtirāʾ and mumārāt both mean contending over something about which there is uncertainty. The root meaning comes from marītu al-nāqah which one says when he rubs a camel’s udder to milk it. Argument is calledmumārāt because of a person arguing (mumāri) persistently in the discussion, draining his opponent of everything he has to say.”

It is said that “outward contention” means keeping the discussion shallow, restricting it to the Qur’anic account and not calling anyone ignorant

or arguing against what they are saying. Alternatively, it is said that an “outward contention” is one which undermines the validity of the opponent’s proof. One says al-mirāʾ al-ẓāhir when his proof is destroyed. It is

also said that ẓahara means that something is remote, as the poet says: Wa tilka shakāt ẓāhirun ʿanka ʿāruhā

This is a complaint, the disgrace of which is remote from you.

The verse (therefore) means: “Since your Lord knows best, and He has already informed you of their tidings, argue with them only about the youths on the basis of clear argument (muḥajja ẓāhira) without going deeply into the matter, or on the basis of the argument which eliminates their proof (muḥajja dhāhiba li-ḥijjatihim), and do not ask for a definitive statement on the youths from any of them. Your Lord suffices you.”

(18:23–24) And do not say of anything: Surely I will do it tomorrow,unless God (so) pleases; and remember your Lord when you

forget and say: Maybe my Lord will guide me to a nearer course to the right than this.

Regardless of whether this addresses the Prophet alone, or the Prophet and others, it refers to a person who believes he can attribute doing something to himself, either now or in the future.

With its divine teachings, the Qur’an takes the position that there is nothing in existence, be it essence or cause and effect, which does not belong to God alone. He can do to it what He wills and He decides about it what He wills, without anyone being able to reverse His decision. No one can own anything apart from what God allows him to own and (what God) gives him control over, making him only the owner of what He has allowed him to own and in control of only what He has put him in control of. There are numerous Qur’anic verses alluding to this truth, so there is no need to cite them all.

Nothing in the cosmos with any agency or affect—what we call agents, means, and active causes—is independent in its causation. Nor can it act or create an effect without Him. People can only do or effect what God wills them to do, in the sense that He gives them control, instead of taking control away from them and willing the opposite.

In other words, no natural cause is inherently a necessary cause in and of its own self. Instead, it is only a cause because He gives it the ability to engage in cause and effect, and because He does not will the opposite. One could say this is accomplished through Him facilitating the path toward the effect, or through His permission (idhn). Permission is granting ability and removing impediments. Many verses indicate that every action

performed by every agent is contingent on His permission. As He says: Whatever palm tree you cut down or leave standing upon its roots, it is by God’s command. . . (59:5), No affliction comes about but by God’s permission. . . (64:11), As for the good land, its vegetation springs forth (abundantly)

by the permission of its Lord. . . (7:58), And a soul will not die but with the permission of God. . . (3:145),And it is not for a soul to believe except by God’s permission. . . (10:100), And We did not send any messenger except that he should be obeyed by God’s permission. . . (4:64). Along with many other verses.

Those who comprehend the status of their Lord and submit to Him should not see themselves as independent causes of their own actions, independent of anyone else. Instead, they possess what they possess because God has granted them possession; they have control because God has granted them control. All strength belongs to God. If they resolve upon doing something, they should resolve upon trusting in Godas in: . . .So when you have decided, place your trust in God. . . (3:159). When they promise something or tell people about what they are going to do, they should qualify it with “by the permission of God” or “so long as He does not will something else.”

If a mind is already exposed to this Qur’anic truism, then when His words, And do not say of anything: Surely I will do it tomorrow, unless God pleases, come knocking on [the mind’s] door, this is the first meaning that will come to mind, particularly since these words come after an explanation of His oneness, divinity, and lordship; and since the previous verses

say that everything on earth is only an embellishment and that it will be turned into bare ground without herbage.

Since humanity’s deeds are part of everything on earth, it follows that humanity’s deeds are also an embellishment. People’s deeds are like an ornamental garment which envelops them, and by which they are tested—although people believe that they own their deeds.

This is because (the words), And do not say of anything: Surely I will do it tomorrow, unless God pleases, stops people from attributing their actions to themselves, even though, doubtlessly, there is no harm in doing so because, frequently, God attributes actions to His Prophetand to other people. He may even command people to attribute actions to themselves, such as in: . . . My work is for me and your work is for you and. . . (10:41), . . . We shall have our deeds and you shall have your deeds. . . (42:15). Thus, the Holy Qur’an does not reject the idea of attributing actions to the agent per se; rather, it only rejects the idea that an agent is independent in his action and free from His will and His permission. This is what

makes the exception in the clause (unless God pleases) correct.

Thus, it is clear, that (grammatically) the phrase implies a bāʾ of concomitance (bāʾ al-mulābasa)1—an exception “emptied” of all circumstances and all times. Its implied meaning is: “And do not say of anything

(that is, of anything upon which you have resolved), surely I will do it tomorrow in any time or circumstance unless you say God willing—that is, you say, surely I will do it tomorrow if God wills that I do it or unless God wills that I do not do it.” In any event, it means, “if God allows it to be done.”

This is the result of reflecting on the meaning of the verse and it is supported by the end of the verse. However, exegetes have other explanations for the verse as follows:

(1) It means the same thing as the previous explanation, except that there is an elliptic “saying” in the exceptive phrase. The implied meaning is: “Unless you say, God willing.” The omission of “you say” shifis “God willing” to a future meaning, making this God’s way of training and educating His servants to say these words after anything they tell others they are going to do, steering them away from being categorical, in order to prevent them from lying or breaking an oath if they fail to do so due to any impediment.

This explanation is attributed to al-Akhfash.

Comment: The problem with this explanation is that it is an unnecessary contrivance; in addition, the substitution changes the meaning, as

is obvious.

(2) The literal meaning is intended throughout, except that the verbal phrase is substitutable with a verbal noun (al-maṣdar al-muʾawwal

1 Bāʾ is a grammatical particle in Arabic. (Ed.)

ilayh), an yashāʾ Allāh (God pleases). It is intended as an object, rendering a meaning of, “And do not say of anything: ‘Surely I will do it tomorrow,’ unless God pleases and wants, because God only wants acts of obedience.” Thus, it is as if what is being said is: “And do not say of anything: ‘Surely I will do it tomorrow,’ unless it is an act of obedience.” The interdiction is to guide to the best course of action (li-l-tanzīh) and not to indicate impermissibility (li-l-taḥrim), such that an indication could be made that it is

permissible to resolve to do permissible things and talk about it. Comment: The problem with this explanation is that it is based on construing “will” (mashiʾa) as legislative will (irāda tashrīʿiyya). There is no evidence for this and He has never used mashiʾa in this sense. On the other hand, the contingency of actions on His creational will is confirmed and has been used in several places in the Qur’an; for instance, what Moses said to al-Khiḍr1: He said: If God pleases (in shāʾ Allāh), you will find me patient . . . (18:69); what Shuʿayb (Jethro) said to Moses:. . . if God pleases (in shāʾ Allāh), you will find me one of the good ones (28:27); what Ishmael (Ismāʿīl) said to his father: . . . if God pleases (in shāʾ Allāh), you will find me

one of the patient ones (37:102); . . . you shall most certainly enter the Sacred

Mosque, if God pleases (in shāʾ Allāh). . .(48:27) and many other verses. Note: This explanation is based on the fundamentals of the Muʿtazilīs. According to the Muʿtazilīs, the only will God has with regard to His servants’ actions is a legislative will, connected to acts of obedience. However,

both reason and textual evidence reject this proposition.

(3) The exceptive sentence refers to doing but not saying, without any need to draw an inference that anything is implied. It means: “Do not say about anything: ‘Verily I shall act independently in doing something, unless God wills something different by making an impediment appear.’” As the Muʿtazilīs say, a servant performs an act independently unless Godmakes an impediment appear that is stronger than he is. W hat this really means is: “Do not say about doing a thing what the Muʿtazilīs say.”

Comment: The problem with this view is that according to the above (explanation), the exceptive sentence would be more applicable to doing than to saying; so, there is no reason to say that an exceptive sentence

1 Some scholars believe that al-Khiḍr is Elijah, while others say he is Andrea. (Ed.)

cannot refer to doing something. An exceptive sentence refers to doing in many places in the Qur’an without there being any problem in understanding. For instance, quoting Abraham: . . . And I do not fear in any way

those that you set up with Him, unless my Lord pleases . . . (6:80), . . . And it befits us not that we should go back to it, except if God our Lord pleases . . . (7:89), . . . They would not believe unless God pleases. . . (6:111) and many other verses.

Thus, the verse should be construed in a manner which is compatible w ith it. (4) The exceptive sentence refers to all times and the object of “pleases” (yashāʾ) is “saying.” This means: “Do not say that unless God pleases (yashāʾ) that you should say it.” “Pleases” means permits—that is, do not say it unless God allows you to do so.

Comment: The problem with this explanation is that it is contingent upon inferring something—that is, “telling” is implied. However, there is no evidence for this in the wording. Without this inference, it is an imposition of an unknown obligation.

(5) The exceptive sentence refers to “ever,” as in (the verse): . . . abiding in it as long as the heavens and the earth endure, except as your

Lord please. . . (11:108). It means: “Do not ever say that.”

Comment: The problem with this explanation is that it contradicts many verses cited above which attribute both past and future acts to the Prophet and to everyone else and even command the Prophet to attribute his actions to himself; for instance: . . . My work is for me and your work for you. . . (10:41), . . . Say: I will recite to you an account of him (18:83) and

. . . And remember your Lord when you forget. . . (18:24).

The connection and shared context between this verse and the previous verse indicates that “forgetting” means “forgetting to say, God willing.”

Thus, remembering one’s Lord means remembering His status, calling attention to that which is the cause of the exception—that is, He looks after every soul through what it earns; He puts people in possession of their actions and makes them able to do them, making them in control of what He put them in control of and able to do what He made them able to do. The verse means: “W hen you forget to say, ‘God willing’ then remember that you have forgotten to do so, and remember your Lord in such

a manner that you keep in mind that you would have done it, had you remembered—surrendering authority and power to Him and qualifying all actions with His permission and His will.”

Because the instruction to remember (dhikr) God is unqualified, it is not restricted to any particular wording. W hat is called for is remembering Him in a specific capacity whether (a) with the clause “unless

God pleases”—appending it to what one has said when one remembers it and has not finished speaking, or (b) repeating what one has said and acknowledging that it is only if God pleases, or (c) after either a short or long pause, referring back pronominally to what one has just said before acknowledging that it is only if God pleases. Some narrations say that when the verses were revealed, the Prophet said: “God willing” or he remembered Him by seeking forgiveness, or something similar.

It is now clear from the above that the following explanations offered by others are incorrect (because):

First, that the verse is independent of the preceding ones, and that forgetting means forgetting Him or any kind of forgetfulness, rendering a meaning of: Remember your Lord when you forget Him, then remember Him, or, Remember your Lord when you forget anything.

Second, based on the first explanation, what is meant by remembering Him is exclusively by saying “unless God pleases,” even after a long pause, or exclusively seeking His forgiveness, or regretting one’s negligence. And say: Maybe my Lord will guide me to a nearer course to the right than this: Here, too, the principle of continuity and the shared context of a duty being imposed in the previous verses dictate that the relative pronoun “this” (hādhā) should refer to remembering after forgetting, rendering a meaning of: “Hope that your Lord will guide you to something nearer to the right than forgetting before remembering”—that is, always remembering without ever forgetting. Thus, it is like the verses calling him (the

Prophet) to always remember, such as: And remember your Lord within yourself humbly and fearing and in a voice not loud in the morning and in the evening, and be not of the heedless ones (7:205).

Mentioning something every time one forgets and then remembers, and keeping at it time and again is one of the means by which one always remembers it.

It is astonishing that exegetes have taken (the pronoun) “this”(hādhā) in the verse to refer to the reports of the Companions of the Cave and have said that the verse means: “Say: Maybe my Lord will give me signs signaling my prophethood better at guiding people than the reports of the Companions of the Cave.” The problem with this explanation is obvious. Even more astonishing than that is what others say—that (the pronoun) “this”(hādhā) refers to what one has forgotten and that the verse

means: “If you forget something, pray to God to remind you of it, and ask your Lord if He does not remind you of what you have forgotten to guide you to something better and more useful than what you have forgotten.” Still more astonishing is what others say—that the clause, and say: Maybe my Lord will guide me, isintroduced by a conjunction explanatory to, and remember your Lord when you forget, meaning: “When you forget, repent to your Lord by saying: Maybe my Lord will guide me to a nearer course to the right than this.” The second and third explanations could be turned into a single explanation; they are both contingent upon “when you forget” meaning, forgetting anything, but the reader will already have realized the problem with that.

(18:25) And they remained in their cave three hundred years and they added (another) nine.

This clarifies how long they remained asleep in the cave. This stay is what is meant in the verses telling the story. The length of their stay was referred to vaguely in the initial verses, Then We veiled their hearing for numbered years in the cave.

This is supported by what follows it: Say: God knows best how long they remained, plus, recite what has been revealed to you, followed by, and say: The truth is from your Lord, coupled with the fact that He does not mention any other figure. Thus, saying, God knows best how long they remained,

after stating the figure is like saying: “My Lord knows best their number” and it alludes to the correctness of the stated figure.

One should not pay attention to the view that the clause, And they remained in their cave, is a quote from the People of the Book, whereas, God knows best how long they remained, is a response to them. Similarly, one should not pay attention to the view that, And they remained. . . and they add (another) nine, is an allusion to the opinion of the People of the Book, the pronoun referring back to them, meaning that the People of the Book added nine years to the actual figure; and then,Say: God knows best how long they remained, is a response to that.

What is narrated from the People of the Book is that the Companions of the Cave remained two hundred years or less, not three hundred and nine, or even three hundred.

Sinīn (years) is not a specifying complement to the number. Otherwise, it [the verse] would have said, thalatha miʾatin sana (lit. three hundred “year” instead of three hundred “years”).1 Rather, it is in apposition to thalāthamiʾatin (three hundred), as they say. There is in the words a similarity to the indeterminate, sinīna ʿadadan (numbered years) at the beginning of the verses.

Perhaps the aim of substituting sinīn (years) for sana (year) is to show that they tarried for a long time (from our perspective). Thus saying “and (some) add (another) nine” implies a sense of juxtaposition as if to say, “and they remained in their cave for three hundred years that seemed so long that some added another nine.” This does not contradict what was explained before with regard to sinīna ʿadadan (a limited or counted number of years) which was mentioned to show how few the years were because the aim behind each of the two sections is different. In the prior section, the aim was to deny that there was anything amazing about the divine sign in the cave when compared with the divine sign shown by making everything on earth an embellishment for it. Thus, it was more appropriate to show how meagre the time period was. However, in this section, the aim is to show that their sojourn in the cave was one of His signs and was a proof against those who denied the resurrection; thus, it is more appropriate to describe the time period as long. The time period can be described in either way (short or long) depending on which perspective it is seen from—it is a paltry thing from His perspective but a

long time from our perspective.

Adding nine years to three hundred years—the length of their stay— gives the outcome that they remained in their cave for three hundred solar years because the difference between three hundred solar years and three hundred lunar years is approximately nine years. There should not be any doubt that the verse means lunar years by sinīn (years) because a sana (year) in Qur’anic convention is a lunar year made up of the months which begin with the new moon. They are what count in the Islamic shariah.

1 A specifying complement (mumayyiz) to a number between 3 and 10 is plural but a specifying complement to a number over 10 is singular. Because the word sinīna (years) is in apposition, this rule does not apply and so it is plural. (Ed.)

Al-Tafsīr al-kabīr disapproves of this strongly because the two figures do not correspond exactly and (the author) challenges what is narrated on the authority of ʿAlī on the matter, even though the difference between three hundred solar years and three hundred and nine lunar years is less than three months. Approximation like this is common in speech.

(18:26) Say: God knows best how long they remained; to Him are (known) the unseen things of the heavens and of the earth; how clear His sight and how clear His hearing! There is none to be a guardian for them besides Him, and He does not make anyone His associate in His Judgment.

This is a continuation of the story about the Companions of the Cave. It refers to the people’s disagreement among themselves over the matter and to the fact that what God related of their story is the truth, about which there is no doubt.

Say: God knows best how long they remained, suggests that—according to the previous verse—the people were not certain how long they

remained in the cave so the Prophet was instructed to argue the point on the basis of God’s knowledge—that He knows them (and their situation) better than anyone else.

To Him (lahu) belong the unseen things of the heavens and the earth, explains that He knows best how long they remained. Lahu (to Him) indicates exclusive possession. It means that He alone owns everything in the unseen realm, in the heavens and on the earth, nothing eludes Him, even if it eludes the heavens and the earth, because He owns the unseen in the true meaning of the word “owns.” He has perfect sight and perfect hearing so He knows best how long they remained—which is part of what is unseen.

Thus, how clear His sight (abṣar), and, how clear His hearing (asmiʿ), both of which are exclamations, mean how perfect His sight and hearing are! These complete the reasoning as if to say: “How can He not know best how long they remained, when He placed them among the unseen and He possesses the unseen, and He saw their situation and heard what they said?”

Some say that lahu (to Him) indicates that God alone knows; that is, the unseen is His in terms of knowledge. This proves that He knows all other creations (that is, non-unseen creations) because if we acknowledge that He has knowledge of the unseen, we can be certain that He knows everything else.

Comment: This is incorrect because the intention of (the words) “how clear His sight and how clear His hearing!” as explained above most likely refers to something novel, and does not emphasize something already said. Similarly, the literal meaning of lahu is complete possession, not just knowledge.

The phrase, There is none to be a guardian for them besides Him, and He does not make anyone His associate in His judgment, denies that anyone has guardianship over them other than God. This includes both independent and dependent guardianship; that is, guardianship independent of God, or by way of the guardianship being delegated by God to someone else. Because a verb (“make”) is used instead of an adjective, the second phrase (He does not make . . .) indicates, through its construction, that the first phrase also denies that anyone else has guardianship other than Him, whether independently or through delegation (that is, whether the guardian would manage their affairs other than God, or whether the guardian were put in charge).

The second phrase denies that God made anyone an associate in ruling or judgment in such a manner that God would be their guardian and

delegate matters and governance to them, the way that rulers appoint governors and commissioners in various areas to handle governance directly

without the knowledge of the rulers.

The phrase can be taken to mean: “How can He not know best how long they remained if He alone is their guardian and He Himself passes judgment among and over them?” The pronoun (them) in lahum (for them) refers to the Companions of the Cave or to everything in the heavens and the earth, as understood from the previous phrase, which puts

rational beings first before everything in the heavens and the earth. The three explanations are in order of their appropriateness, the first one being the best.

Thus the verse incorporates two proofs that God knows best how long they remained. First, applicable both to them (the Companions of the Cave) and to everything else, to Him (lahu) belong the unseen things of the heavens and the earth; how clear His sight and how clear His hearing! So He knows best everything, including how long the Companions

of the Cave remained. Second, a proof exclusive to them—that is, There is none to be a guardian for them, because God is their guardian, directly responsible for the judgment passed over them, so how can He not know better than anyone else? The two sentences are separate and not joined with a conjunction because their aim is different.

Examining Narrations

(1) About the verse,Or do you think that the Companions of the Cave. . ., Tafsīr al-Qummī says (it means):

“We have brought you signs more amazing than it. They were youths who lived in the period between Jesus son of Maryam and Muḥammad. The Inscription was two copper plaques which were marqūm—that is, they were inscribed with the account of the youths and how they submitted to God, what King Decius wanted from them, and what happened to them and transpired with them.”

(2) The same book (Tafsīr al-Qummī) says:

My father told me on the authority of Ibn Abī ʿUmayr on the authority of Abū Baṣīr on the authority of Abū ʿAbdillāh:

The reason Surat al-Kahfiwas revealed was because Quraysh sent three people to Najrān: al-Naḍr b. al-Ḥārith b. Kaldah, ʿUqbah b. Abī Muʿīt, and al-ʿĀs b. Wāʾil al-Sahmī to learn from the Jews what they should ask God’s Messenger.

So they set offfor Najrān (and went) to the Jewish rabbis, and they said: “Ask him three questions; if he answers you in accordance with what we say, he is telling the truth. Then ask him a single question to which, if he claims to know the answer, he is lying.” They asked: “What are these questions?”

They replied: “Ask him about the youths in the prior era who went away, stayed away, and fell asleep. How long did they remain asleep before waking up? How many of them were there? What was with them besides themselves? What was their story? Ask him about Moses when God commanded him to follow the scholar and learn from him. Who was he? How did he follow him? What was his story with him? Ask him about the one who set out where the sun sets and rises until he reached Gog and Magog’s barrier.

Who was he? What was his story?”

They then told them the tidings of these three questions, saying: “If he answers as we have dictated, he is telling the truth, but if he tells you something different, do not believe him.”

They asked: “What is the fourth question?”

They replied: “Ask him when the Hour will be. If he claims knowledge of it, he is lying because no one else but blessed and almighty

God knows when the Hour will be.”

Thereafter, they returned to Mecca and gathered before Abū Ṭālib, saying: “Abū Ṭālib, your nephew claims that tidings from heaven come to him. We will ask him questions; if he answers them, we will know that he is telling the truth, but if he does not answer us, we will know he is lying.”

Thereafter, Abū Ṭālib replied: “Ask him whatever seems proper to you,” and so they asked him the three questions.

God’s Messenger replied: “I will answer you tomorrow without any exception.”

Thereafter, revelation was withheld from him for forty days until the Prophet felt worried and his Companions who had believed in him had doubt. The Quraysh rejoiced, and mocked and annoyed them, and Abū Tālib was sorrowful.

Then, after forty days, Surat al-Kahfiwas revealed, and so God’s Messenger said: “Gabriel, you took your time.” He replied: “We can only reveal by God’s permission.”

Thereafter, God revealed: “Or do you think, O Muḥammad that out of all Our signs the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription were an amazing sign of Ours?” He then related their story, saying: “When the youths sought refuge in the cave, they said: Our Lord! grant us mercy from You, and provide for us a right course in our affair.”

(3) The same book (Tafsīr al-Qummī) quotes Imam al-Ṣādiq as saying: The Companions of the Cave and the Inscription lived during the time of a tyrannical, violent king who enjoined his subjects to worship idols. He would kill whoever failed to do so. They were a group of believers who worshiped God, mighty and sublime is He. The king put people in charge of the city gates to prevent anyone from leaving the city without prostrating to the idols.

Thus, they set out on the pretext of hunting. They passed a shepherd on their way and invited him to their religion, but he did

not respond. However, he had a dog with him; it did (respond), and went offwith them.1

Thereafter, the Companions of the Cave set offfrom the city on the pretext of going hunting (but were actually) fleeing from that king’s religion. Then, when evening fell, they entered that cave, their dog with them, and Godcast that soporific over them, as God says: Then We veiled their hearing for a limited number of years in the cave. And then they slept until God made that king and the people of the city perish. That era passed and another era came, along with other people.

Then, when they woke up, they said to each other: “How long have we been asleep here?” They looked at the sun which had risen and said: “A day or part of a day.” Then, they said to one of them: “Take this silver coin and enter the city secretly—without their recognizing you—and buy us food because if they know about us and recognize us, they will kill us or force us back into their religion.”

That man went and saw the city was different from what he was used to and saw people different from before whom he did not know, who did not know his language, and whose language he did not know. They then asked him: “Who are you? Where have you come from?” He told them, and so the king of that city set offwith his companions, accompanied by the man, before stopping at the opening of the cave.

They began looking in and some of them said: There are three of them and the dog is their fourth. Others said: Five and the dog is their sixth. Others said: Seven and the dog is their eighth. God enveloped them with awe, rendering them all, except their companion, unable to go in to them. When he went in to them, he

found them fearful that it was Decius’ cohorts they had heard.

Their companion told them that they had been asleep for a long time and that they were a sign for the people. They then wept and asked God to put them back to sleep as they were in their resting places.

The king then said: “We should build a place of prostration here for us to visit them because they were a group of believers.” They were turned twice every year, sleeping on their right side for six months and their lefiiside for the other six months, their dog with them throughout, stretching its paws out in the wide open space in the cave, as He said: “We relate to you their story with truth.” Author’s comment: Of all the traditions narrating the story, this is one of the clearest worded and freest of falsification. However, in spite of that, it says that those who disagreed over how many of them there were— by saying three, five or seven—were the people of the city who gathered around the opening to the cave after the youths woke up; this contradicts the literal meaning of the verse. It also says that the Companions of the Cave did not die the second time. Instead it says that they went back to sleep, as did their dog, stretching out its paws in the wide open space within the cave; and, also, that they continued to be turned twice a year from right to lefiiand vice versa, remaining as they were, even though there is no known cave like this on the face of the earth with people sleeping in it.

Besides, the end of this narration—which we have refrained from citing here, fearing that it is the words of al-Qummī or another narration—says that (the words), And they remained in their cave three hundred

years and (some) add (another) nine, is what the People of the Book said and that, Say: God knows best how long they remained, was a response to them. The reader will already have realized from our explanation above that this is refuted by the context, and that it would not be an acceptably eloquent form of composition.

Both sects (Sunnī and Shī‘ah) report many narrationsexplaining the story. However, the narrations are contradictory and there are discrepancies, such that two narrations with exactly the same content in all respects

can scarcely be found.

Part of this discrepancy is what some of the narrations say about the four questions. Some say the four questions were about the Companions of the Cave, Moses and the scholar, Dhū l-Qarnayn, and when the Hour will come.

Others say that the questions were about the Companions of the Cave, Dhū l-Qarnayn, and the soul (that is, only three questions are mentioned). They (that is, the Jewish rabbis) said that the sign of the Prophet’s

truthfulness would be his not answering the last question. So he (that is, the Prophet) answered about the Companions of the Cave and Dhū l-Qarnayn, but because the verse: . . . Say: The soul is one of the commands of my Lord . . . (17:85) was revealed, he did not answer the last question. The reader will already have realized from the explanation of the “verse of the soul” (āyat al-rūḥ, in Ar. vol. 13) that the wording (in verse 17:85) is formulated as an answer and not as a rebuke.

Another example is that some narrations say that there was just one group known both as the Companions of the Cave and of the Inscription, whereas others say that the Companions of the Inscription were not the same as the Companions of the Cave, and that God alluded to them together in His words, but only told the story of the Companions of the Cave and eschewed telling the story of the Companions of the Inscription. They tell a story about them—they were a group of three who went out foraging for their family but the heavens came down upon them, and so they sought refuge in a cave. A rock from the top of the mountain fell down and blocked offthe exit.

They said to each other that each of them should make mention of some of his good deeds so that God might free them. Thereafter, one of them cited his work for God’s sake and prayed to God seeking the intercession of his work, and the rock moved enough to let in some light. Then

the second did the same and the rock moved enough for them to be able to see each other. Then the third did the same, and God freed them, and so they escaped.

Nuʿman b. Bashīr cites this1 without stating the chain of narration and attributing it (marfūʿan) to the Prophet.

Anyone familiar with the style of the Qur’an (lit. the “wise remembrance”) will refuse to contemplate the idea that it alludes to two different

stories only to go into detail about one of them and completely forget the other one.

Another example is that some narrations say that the king from whom

the youths fled was the Roman Emperor Diocletian (285–305 CE); others say that he claimed to be a god; and others say that he was the Roman Emperor Decius (249–254 CE), even though there are decades between the two. The king enjoined idolatry and the killing of monotheists. Other narrations say that he was a Zoroastrian propagating the Zoroastrian religion, even though history does not record that Zoroastrianism spread into the Byzantine Empire. Other narrations say that it happened in the time before Jesus.

Another example is that some narrations say that al-Raqīm was the name of the city they lef ; others, that it was the name of the valley; others, that it was the name of the mountain the cave was in; others, that it

Others say that it was placed inside it, others say that it was hung above the city gate, others say that it was in one of the king’s vaults, and others say that there were two plaques. Another example is that some narrations say that the youths were children of the king and children of noblemen; others, that they were the children of scholars; others, that there were seven of them, the seventh being

a shepherd who, along with his dog, tagged along with them on the way. Wahb b. Munabbih’s narration1 says that they were bathhouse attendants who worked in one of the city’s bathhouses; this narration tells the

Another example is that some narrations say that they showed their opposition, and the king realized it before they lef . Others say that he only found out about it after they had lef . Others say that they colluded in leaving and lef . Others say that they lefiiwithout knowing each other and without prearranging it, but subsequently got to know each other and reached an agreement in the desert. Others say that a shepherd tagged along with them, as their seventh, others say that he did not follow them but his dog did and traveled with them.

Another example is that some narrations say that when they fled and the king looked into their affair, the king could not find them or any trace

Others say that he searched for them, found them sleeping in the cave, and ordered that an edifice be built at the entrance to the cave, trapping them, so that they would die of starvation and dehydration as punishment for their disobedience. Thereafter, they remained like that until, when God wanted to awaken them, He sent a shepherd who knocked down the edifice to build a pen for his sheep. At that time, God roused them and what happened to them was as per the story told by God.

Another example is that some narrations say that when their affair became known, the king came with some people and went in to talk to them in the cave. While he was talking to them and they were talking to him, all of a sudden they bade him farewell, wished him peace, and passed away. Others say that they died or went back to sleep before the king went in to see them, the entrance to the cave was blocked off, and they disappeared from sight without their being able to find a way in to see them.

Thereafter, they built a masjid (mosque) to pray in.

Another example is that some of the narrations say that their souls were taken. Others say that God made them sleep a second time, and they will remain asleep until the Day of Resurrection, and that He turns them twice a year—from right to lefiiand vice versa.

Another example is that the narrations disagree over the length of their stay. Most say they remained three hundred and nine years as stated in the verse in the words of God. Others say—that is what the People of the Book said with, God knows best how long they remained, being a response to them. Some say that three hundred years was what He said, and it was the People of the Book who added another nine.

There are other discrepancies between the narrations. We have collected most of the Sunnī narrations from al-Durr al-manthūr and the

Shia narrations from Bihār al-anwār, al-Burhān fī tafsīr al-Qurʾān, and Tafsīr nūr al-thaqalayn. Anyone who wants to scrutinize (the narrations) further should refer to them.

What the narrations can be said to agree upon or reach a quasi-agreement upon is the fact that they were a group of monotheists who fled

from a tyrannical king who forced people to attribute partners to God, so they sought refuge in the cave, slept, and so on, up to the end of the story told by God.

Author’s comment: It may be stated that the literal meaning of His words, When they stood up and said: Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth; we will by no means call upon any god besides Him, is that they did not believe in dissimulation (taqiyya), as some exegetes believe to be possible based on His words, or force you back to their religion, and then you will never succeed, as stated above.

However, this is not the case, for the reader will already have realized that their departure from the city was a flight from the abode of polytheism, in which they were prevented from proclaiming the word of truth

and practising monotheism. When six noble people who knew each other planned together to leave, and turned their backs on their people, property, and homeland, this could not be called anything else but opposing

idolatry. They would have been in great danger if the people had prevailed against them and they would have come to one of two lots—being stoned to death or forced back into the people’s religion.

Thus it is clear that when they originally stood up and said, Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth; we will by no means call upon any god besides Him, this was not an open form of opposition by them. Nor was it a public condemnation of the people’s religion or an assault on their way, because the general situation did not allow them to do so. They were choosing the side of God, resolving to remain firm in monotheism. If it is conceded that, when they stood up and said: Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, means that they went to the public and refused to hide their belief, that would have been during the last days of their time among the people. Before that, they would inevitably have been hiding their belief. Thus it is clear that nothing in the context of the two verses contradicts the idea that the youths hid their belief (that is, they engaged in taqiyya) throughout the time they were among the people and in the city. (10) Tafsīr al-ʿAyyāshī also relates from Abū Bakr al-Ḥaḍramī from Abū ʿAbdillāh (Imam al-Ṣādiq):

“The Companions of the Cave set offwithout knowing each other and without any prior agreement. When they reached the desert, they made covenants and pacts with each other. (11) The following narration on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās says the same thing:

Al-Durr al-manthūr, citing Ibn Shayba, Ibn al-Mundhir and Abū Ḥātim on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās:

Muʿāwiya then said: “If only they were shown to us and we could see them.”

Ibn ʿAbbās replied: “This is not for you. Godforbade that to someone who was better than you, and He said: ‘If you looked at them you would certainly turn back from them in flight, and you would certainly be filled with awe because of them.’”

He (Ibn ʿAbbās) said: “They were in one of the tyrannical kings’

kingdoms and the people began worshiping (different things)

until they began worshiping idols. These youths were in the city. When they saw that, they lefiithat city, so Godbrought them together without prior agreement. He (Ibn ʿAbbās) said: “They stayed, and so people came looking for them, not knowing where they had gone. They raised the matter with the king, and he said: ‘Those people will be of significance

after today—people who lefiiwithout anyone knowing where they have gone, without any betrayal, and without any information on them.’ He then called for a lead plaque and wrote their names on it, then threw it in his vault. That is what, or do you think that the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription, means; the inscription was the plaque on which they were written about. So they

set offbefore finally entering the cave, and then God veiled their hearing and they slept. If the sun shone on them, it would burn them, and if they were not turned, the ground would eat into them. That is what, And you might see the sun. . ., means.”

He (Ibn ʿAbbās) said: “That king then passed on, and another king came along. He worshiped God, forsaking those idols, and was fair with the people. Thus, God roused them for His purpose, one of them asking: ‘How long have you tarried?’ One of them replied: ‘A day.’ Another said: ‘Two days.’ Another said: ‘More than that.’ Their eldest said: ‘Do not disagree among yourselves because no people have ever disagreed among themselves without being doomed. Rather, send one of yourselves with this silver coin of yours to the city.’”

“He saw clothes that he did not recognize and buildings he did not recognize. He then approached a baker and tossed him a silver coin. Their dirhams had the imprint of young camels and the baker did not recognize the silver coin. He asked: ‘Where did you get this silver coin from? You’ve found a stash? Show it to me. Otherwise I’ll report you to the amir.’”

“He (the messenger) asked: ‘Are you threatening me with the amir?’”

“And so he came to amir who was in charge. He (the amir) asked:

‘Who is your father’? He replied ‘so-and-so,’ but he did not know him. He asked: ‘Who is the king?’ He said ‘so-and-so,’ but he did not know him. The people gathered around him, and so he brought it up with their scholar. He asked him and he told him.

1. The Story of the Companions of the Cave in the Narrations The full story appears in detail in a number of narrations from the Companions (sahāba), successors (tābiʿīn), and Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt, such as the narrations from al-Qummī, Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, and Mujāhid. It is told in al-Durr al-manthūr and Ibn Isḥāq’s narration in al-ʿArāʾis cited in al-Burhān, Wahb b. Munabbih’s narration cited in al-Durr al-manthūr, in al-Kāmil without any attribution, and Nuʿmān b. Bashīr’s narration on the Companions of the Inscription set out in al-Durr al-manthūr.

These narrations, some of which are cited in the discussion on the relevant narrations (above) and others which we alluded to differ so much in their wording that they barely agree with each other on any of the important aspects of the story. The discrepancy between them is even greater in the narrations on particular aspects of the story, such as those dealing with the time in which they rose up (against) the king, the king in whose reign they rose up, their lineage, their characteristics, their names, the reason they were called the Companions of the Inscription, and all the other details of the story. Arriving at anything that one can be sure of is even more difficult.

The main reasons for the discrepancy between these narrations apart from the fabrication and interpolation which has crept into narrations like them are [outlined below]:

1) The People of the Book devoted a lot of attention to this story, as can be inferred from the narrations about it; the Quraysh heard it from them and asked the Prophet about it. In fact, it can be understood from depictions cited by historians on the authority of the Christians and from paintings found in caves in various parts of the world—Asia, Europe, and Africa—that the story gained an element of international renown. It is in the nature of such stories that they manifest to every people in a form compatible with their own opinions and beliefs, and accounts of it vary accordingly.

Moreover, the Muslims were excessively enthusiastic in hearing the story, recording it, and embellishing it. They took what others had, just as they took what they themselves had, especially given that a number of scholars from the People of the Book, such as Wahb b. Munabbih and Kaʿb al-Aḥbar, had become Muslims, and the Companions and successors acquired the tidings of previous generations from them in large quantity. Thereafter the later Muslims learned these legends from the early Muslims and treated their narrations like the ones lefiias a legacy by the Prophet so it was a disaster.

2) It is God’s custom in narrating stories only to select the important points which will be effective in achieving the (divine) purpose without going into detail, mentioning everything, or addressing all of the facets, lives, and times contemporary to the stories. God’s book is not a history book. It is naught but a book of guidance.

This is one of the most obvious things which will be stumbled across by anyone reflecting on the aforementioned stories in His word, including the story of the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription. God first cites a line of their conversation alluding to the reason for their uprising for His sake; then how they remained firm upon the word of truth; then how they forsook the people after that; and then how they entered the cave and slept there, their dog with them throughout the long period. He then mentions how they were awakened from their sleep and a second conversation they had, leading to their situation becoming known to the people.

He then mentions how the people stumbled across them, how their souls were taken a second time after the divine purpose was achieved, and what was done after that—a mosque (masjid) was built over them. This is what His words encompass.

He avoids citing their names, lineages, dates of birth, their upbringings, the work they took on, their positions in society, when they rose up,

the details of them forsaking their people, the name of the king whom they fled, the city they lef , the people they used to live among, the name of the dog which kept close to them, whether it was a hunting dog or sheepdog and what its color was, even though the narrations assiduously mention these details as well as other matters which are not necessary to know for the purpose of guidance, although they are the aim of historical investigation.

Then, when early Muslim exegetes began studying the verses telling the story, they wanted to explain how the verses were linked by adding the bits lefiiout of the story to what had been selected and taken so that the whole story could be composed. Thus, the difference in their opinions led to discrepancies as in the narratives, and the matter led to what

we see today.

2. The story of the Companions of the Cave in the Qur’an God said, addressing the Prophet in the second person: Therefore contend not in the matter of them but with an outward contention (18-22). The Companions of the Cave and the Inscription were youths who grew up in a polytheistic society that only believed in worshiping idols. Thereafter, monotheism spread into the society and a group of them believed in God. They were condemned for it and confronted with force, pressure, strife, and punishment. They were forced to worship the idols and reject monotheism. Whoever returned to their religion would be lefiialone, but whoever continued to resist would be killed in the worst possible way. The youths were among those who had propagated belief in God, so God increased them in guidance, effused them with knowledge and wisdom, and revealed what was important to them through the light He had

given them. He strengthened their hearts, and so they feared God alone and were not deterred by the incidents and dangers they were faced with. They realized that if they continued to remain in the ignorant despotic society, they would have no recourse but to follow their way of life, unable to utter the word of truth or follow the true shariah. They realized that what they had to do was to rise up on the basis of monotheism, reject polytheism, and forsake the people. They realized that if they forsook them and took refuge in the cave, God would save them from the trial they were enduring.

They then stood up and said to the people regarding their imperiousness and despotism: Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth; we

will by no means call upon any god besides Him, for then indeed we should have said an extravagant thing. These our people have taken gods besides Him; why do they not produce any clear authority in their support? Who is then more unjust than the one who forges a lie against God? (18:14–15). They then said: And when you forsake them and what they worship save God, betake yourselves for refuge to the cave; your Lord will extend to you largely of His mercy and provide for you a profitable course in your affair (18:16).

Thereafter, they entered the cave and settled down in a wide space within it, their dog stretching its paws out in the open space. They then petitioned their Lord with what they had previously recognized that He would do to them, saying: Our Lord! Grant us mercy from You, and provide for us a right course in our affair (18:10).

So God veiled their hearing for (numbered) years in the cave, and they remained in their cave—their dog with them—three hundred years and (some) add (another) nine. And you might see the sun when it rose, it would decline from their cave toward the right hand, and when it set, it would leave them behind on the lefiiwhile they were in a wide space thereof . . . And you might think them awake while they were asleep and Godturned them about to the right and to the lef , while their dog (lay) outstretching its paws in the wide open space; if you looked at them you would certainly turn back from them in flight, and you would certainly be filled with awe because of them.

Next, God roused them after this long time—three hundred and nine years from the day they entered the cave, to show them how He had saved them from their people. Then they all woke up and found that the sun had changed position. They were lethargic from their heavy sleep: A speaker among them said: How long have you tarried? (18:19) They said: We have tarried for a day or part of a day (18:19), because of the change in the sun’s position they saw, and so they wavered over whether a night had passed or not. Others among them said: Your Lord knows best how long you have tarried (18:19). One of them then said: Now send one of you with this silver (coin) of yours to the city, then let him see which of them has the purest

food, so let him bring you provision from it (18:19),for you are hungry, and let the one among you who goes to the city behave with gentleness in his journey there and in buying the food, and by no means make your case known to anyone:For surely if they prevail against you (that is, knew your position) they would stone you to death or force you back to their religion, and then you will never succeed (18:19–20).

This was the time for God to have the people stumble across them because the people they had forsaken and lefiithe day they entered the cave had perished. God had made them, their kingdom, and their religion perish, and brought along other people, most of whom were authoritative monotheists. They—that is, the monotheists and the others, had a

disagreement over the matter of resurrection, and God wanted to show them a sign with regard to that. He then made them stumble across the Companions of the Cave.

The youths’ emissary set offand came to the city, thinking that it was in the same condition they had lefiiit the previous day. However he found that the city had changed unlike anything ever seen in a day or a lifetime: the people were not the same, and the situation and circumstances were different from those seen the previous day. He remained confused about the matter until he wanted to buy some food with the silver coin he had with him—the currency of three centuries gone by—and so a dispute broke out over it. Without any ado, an amazing thing became apparent— that the youth was one of those who had lived there three centuries ago; he was one of the youths who had lived among the oppressive polytheists and who had subsequently fled their homes, forsaken their people to

defend their faith, and entered the cave. God had then made them sleep for this long period before rousing them. Now, they were still in the cave, awaiting this one whom they had sent to the city to buy food for them to take their repast upon.

The news immediately spread in the city, and a large crowd of its inhabitants gathered around. They then set offto the cave along with the youth sent by his companions. What they saw confirmed what the youth had said about his companions and the divine sign with regard to the matter of the resurrection was manifested to them.

It was not long after the Companions of the Cave were awakened that caused them to pass away. At that point, the inhabitants of the city gathered at the entrance to the cave, once again disagreeing among themselves. The polytheists said: Erect an edifice over them—their Lord knows

them best (18:21).

The monotheists [those who prevailed in their affair] said: We will certainly raise a mosque over them (18:21).

3. The story according to non-Muslims

According to most storytellers and historians, the incident took place during the period between the Prophet and Jesus. That is the reason it is not mentioned in the Old or New Testament and why it did not originate with the Jews, even though a number of narrations say that the Quraysh heard the story from the Jews. It was only the Christians who cared about it and who told it, then and now. Whatis narrated from them is close to what Ibn Isḥāq cites in al-ʿArāʾis on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās except that their accounts differ from those of the Muslims on a number of issues: 1) The Syriac sources state that there were eight Companions of the Cave, whereas Muslim sources, and similarly Greek and western ones say that there were seven.

2) The story does not mention the dog belonging to the Companions of the Cave.

3) They state that the length of time the Companions of the Cave remained there was two hundred years or less, whereas most Muslims state that it was three hundred and nine years according to the literal meaning of the Noble Qur’an. The reason they say that is because they say the tyrant who forced people to worship idols and from whom the youths fled was Emperor Decius (449–451). According to what they say, the Companions of the Cave woke up in 435, 437, or 439 CE, so they could only have been in the cave for two hundred years or less. It is said that the first historian among them to mention the story was Jacob of Saruq, the Syriac who was born in the year 451 and died in the year 521. Others then took this from him. There is more to say and it will follow.

4. Where is the cave?

A number of caves and grottos have been excavated in various parts of the world with paintings on their walls of three, five, or seven men along with a dog. Some of them show that they are sacrificing something. A person looking at them will think of the story of the Companions of the Cave and might suppose that these engravings and images are an allusion to their story. After the story appeared in various regions, it spread and circulated and was used as a reminder for monks and hermits to worship in these caves.

People disagree over precisely which cave the youths sought refuge in and hid in. It is claimed to be in a number of different places, as follows. The first cave is the one in Ephesus, which is a ruined archaeological city in Turkey 73 kilometers from the town of Izmir. The cave is one

kilometer or less from Ephesus near the township of Selçuk at the foot of Mount Pion (Panayır Dağı).

It is a wide cave containing—as it is said—hundreds of graves built from clay bricks and it is at the foot of the mountain. The entrance faces northeast, but there is no trace of any mosque, hermitage, or church. This cave is the most well-known according to the Christians and it is mentioned in several Muslim narrations. In spite of this cave’s great popularity,

the features mentioned in the Qur’an do not pertain to it.

First, God said: And you might see the sun when it rose, it would decline from their cave toward the right hand, and when it set, it would leave them behind on the lef (18:17), which explicitly indicates that the sun’s rays fall to the right of the cave at sunrise and to its lefiiat sunset. This means that the cave’s entrance must face south, whereas the entrance to the cave at Ephesus faces northeast.

The fact that the entrance to the cave at Ephesus faces north, along with what is said about where the sun’s rays fall at sunrise and sunset, is what led exegetes to think that the right and lefiiofithe cave are from the perspective of someone entering as opposed to leaving the cave, even though the latter is what is customary, as previously mentioned in the exegesis of the relevant verse. al-Bayḍāwī says in his exegesis:

“The entrance to the cave faces the stars on the handle of the Big Dipper, and the closest eastern and western horizons in line with it are east and west of the top of Cancer (the constellation in the zodiac). W hen the sun is on its axis, it shines slanted away from it facing the right side, which is to the west; and it sets in line with its lefiiside, its rays falling to its side, breaking up its putridity and leveling its breeze without affecting them (the Companions of the Cave), harming their bodies, or spoiling their clothes.”

Others say the same as he does. However, because its entrance faces northeast toward the Big Dipper and not the North Pole—as they say— the description does not apply, even from the perspective stipulated by them, because the sun’s rays would fall on the western side adjacent to the entrance at sunrise. At sunset, the entrance and everything around it is shrouded in the shade, the sun’s rays having disappeared far away along with the sun, and the shade having stretched out, unless of course it is claimed that (the words), and when it set (it would) leave them behind on the lef , means the rays not falling, or falling behind them instead of to the lef .

Second, His words, while they were in a fajwa thereof, mean an elevated part, but there is no elevated part in the cave of Ephesus—so they

say—and in any event this is contingent upon fajwa meaning “an elevated part,” which is not necessarily the case. It was stated above that it means a wide space.

Third, the literal meaning of: Those who prevailed in their affair said: We will certainly raise a mosque over them (18:21), is that they raised a mosqueover the cave. However, there is no trace of any mosque, hermitage, or anything else like that at the cave at Ephesus. The closest thing to

it is a church approximately three kilometers away, but there is nothing at all to link it to the cave.

Moreover there is no plaque, writing, or anything else to prove even partially that some of those graves—and there are hundreds of them—are the graves of the Companions of the Cave, or that they remained asleep there for the described period before being awakened before God caused them to pass away.

The second cave is Rajīb Cave, eight kilometers from the Jordanian capital Amman near a village called Rajīb. The cave is in a mountain carved into the rock in its southern foothill. Its edges from the east and west are open, and the sun’s rays fall onto it from them. The entrance to the cave faces south. Inside the cave, there is a small ledge about three meters by two and a half meters that is to the side of the roof of the cave, [which is] three [meters] by three [meters]. There are several graves in the cave in the form of Byzantine sarcophagi—about seven or eight of them. On the walls there are carvings and illegible effaced writing in ancient Greek. There is also a picture of a dog painted red, gold ornaments, and other embellishments.

Above the cave are the remains of a Byzantine hermitage proven by the coins and other remains discovered inside it to have been built during the time of Emperor Justinius I (418–427). Other remains—an Islamic mosque containing a prayer niche (miḥrāb), minaret, and facility to perform basic ablutions—prove that the hermitage was transformed again

after the Muslims seized the land. In the open space opposite the entrance to the cave are the remains of another mosque built by the Muslims at the dawn of Islam. They then built it up and reinforced it repeatedly. It is built upon the ruins of a Byzantine church just like the mosque above the cave.
